title: Metabolomics reveals the hindgut metabolic changes and physiological impacts in weaned piglets subjected to ETEC infection and berberine intervention

sections.abstract:
Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (ETEC) causes diarrhea and triggers intestinal inflammation posing a significant threat to children which is a global health concern. Berberine (BBR) has diverse pharmacological properties can alleviate diarrhea and intestinal damage. This metabolomics study analyzed the effects of berberine on the hepatic function, lipid metabolism, and inflammatory responses in weaned piglet model infected with ETEC. A total of 18 piglets were randomly divided into three groups: basal diet (BD) + Saline, BD + ETEC, and BBR + ETEC. Compared with the BD + Saline group, ETEC infection significantly increased the contents of aspartate aminotransferase (AST), AST/alanine aminotransferase (ALT), total protein, globulin, triglycerides, tumor necrosis factor α (TNF-α), interleukin 1β (IL-1β), IL-6, IL-8, IL-12, interferon γ (IFN-γ), IL-4, IL-10, and transforming growth factor β (TGF-β) and significantly decreased the contents of total cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein (LDL), and high-density lipoprotein (HDL) in the serum of weaned piglets. There were 14 metabolites upregulated and 21 metabolites downregulated after ETEC infection, and total cholesterol, LDL, IL-1β, IL-8, and TGF-β were correlated with fructose and mannose metabolism. Compared with the BD + ETEC group, dietary berberine significantly increased the contents of total cholesterol, LDL, and HDL and significantly decreased the contents of AST, AST/ALT, total protein, globulin, triglycerides, TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, IL-12, IFN-γ, and IL-4 in the serum of weaned piglets. There were 111 metabolites upregulated and 48 metabolites downregulated after berberine addition, and total protein, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, and IL-12 were correlated with cholinergic synapse. Both ETEC infection and berberine addition can induce changes in taste transduction and affect the physiological functions of weaned piglets through metabolic pathways.

The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1038/s41598-025-21011-8.
sections.introduction:
Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (ETEC) can cause diarrhea and trigger intestinal inflammation when the host’s immunity decreases or the intestinal integrity is damaged 1 , 2 . Young animals have poor immunity, especially mammals that have to experience weaning stress so that ETEC can cause considerable harm to human infants and other young mammals 3 , 4 . ETEC infection causing malnutrition and diarrhea in children, affects their growth, and is a serious global health concern 5 . At present, the pathogenic mechanism of ETEC has been studied: ETEC bacteria adhere to the small intestinal epithelial cells and produce enterotoxins leading to metabolic dysfunction and impaired reabsorption. Then, a large amount of water and electrolytes accumulate, eventually leading to diarrhea and dehydration 6 – 8 .

Berberine (BBR) is a plant alkaloid primarily extracted from the Chinese medicinal herb Coptis chinensis and other species within the Berberis genus. It exhibits diverse pharmacological properties, such as anti-inflammatory, anti-infectious, and anti-tumor effects 9 . It is reported that berberine can regulate metabolic disorders, enhance glucose metabolism, and increase the growth performance of piglets 10 , 11 . Further research has indicated that berberine has a positive impact on the intestinal microbiota and can regulate the Nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) and MAPK signaling pathways to inflammatory responses, as well as diarrhea and intestinal damage caused by ETEC 12 , 13 . Berberine has high research value in alleviating bacterial infections and diarrhea caused by ETEC infection.

Metabolomics holds vast potential for elucidating functions within complex systems and broadening our understanding of gut microbial metabolism 14 . Intestinal metabolism includes a variety of small-molecule substances, plays a key role in regulating host immunity and metabolism, and is the main contributor to intestinal inflammation 15 . Therefore, the study of intestinal metabolomics has great potential. Metabolomics has been widely applied in various fields, and many studies have used metabolomics to explore the metabolism of pigs 14 , 16 . Although there is an increasing amount of metabolomics research, metabolomics studies on berberine’s physiological effects in ETEC infection have been limited. Most metabolic processes in animals are similar, so studying the effects of berberine on the metabolism of weaned piglets contributes to determining its complex biological properties and promoting its application in humans. This study established a diarrhea model of piglets with ETEC infection and used colonic metabolomics to explore how the berberine alleviating ETEC infection.
sections.methods:
All animal experiments were conducted in accordance with the guidelines for the care and use of animals and were approved by the Anhui Science and Technology University’s Experimental Animal Ethics Committee (approval number: AHSTU2023006). Written informed consent was obtained in advance from all animal owners prior to sample collection and experimental procedures. In accordance with the editorial policies of Scientific Reports, this study is reported in compliance with the ARRIVE guidelines.

The Escherichia coli F4 (K88 ac) strain was acquired from the National Center for Veterinary Culture Collection of China (CVCC1500).

In this study, a local farm provided 18 crossbred pigs (Duroc × Landrace × Large Yorkshire) to us. The pigs were weaned at 21 days and housed in a controlled environment following established protocols 17 , 18 . Each group contained an equal number of male and female piglets, and there was no significant difference in the average body weight of piglets between groups. They had free access to water and a uniform basic diet. The experiment lasted 24 days, including 21 days for a feeding trial period and 3 days for the ETEC challenge period; a 5-day adaptation period had already been completed beforehand, all piglets were fed a basal diet during the adaptation period, and in the subsequent 24-day experimental period, each group received their respective diets. The diet composition and nutrients for different groups are detailed in Table 1 . A total of three groups were established, with six pigs randomly assigned to each group (Fig. 1 ): BD + Saline (piglets were fed a basal diet and orally administered 10 ml of saline), BD + ETEC (piglets were fed a basal diet and orally administered 10 ml of ETEC), and BBR + ETEC (piglets were fed a basal diet with 0.1% berberine and orally administered 10 ml of ETEC). The concentration of the ETEC suspension used for oral administration was 10⁸ CFU/mL, and the feed used in the experiment was all in granular form. Berberine chloride hydrate (purity ≥ 98%) was obtained from Aladdin Reagent Co., Ltd (Shanghai, China) 19 .

On the morning of Day 25, blood was drawn from the piglets’ external jugular vein before feeding. The samples were placed in coagulation tubes and centrifuged at 3,000 g for 10 min at 4 °C. The resulting serum was stored at − 80 °C. After euthanasia, mid-colonic contents sample were collected during dissection and similarly preserved at − 80 °C for subsequent metabolomics analysis.

The contents of alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), alkaline phosphatase (ALP), total protein, albumin, globulin, total cholesterol, triglycerides, low-density lipoprotein (LDL), and high-density lipoprotein (HDL) in serum were quantified using an automated biochemical analyzer (model B31614 ). The contents of tumor necrosis factor α (TNF-α), interleukin 1β (IL-1β), IL-6, IL-8, IL-12, interferon γ (IFN-γ), IL-4, IL-10, and transforming growth factor β (TGF-β) in serum were quantified using ELISA kits (Beijing Daktronics Technology Co., Ltd., Beijing, China) in accordance with the manufacturer’s protocol.

Metabolomics analysis was performed using liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS), and the KEGG database was used for the annotation of the detected metabolites 20 – 22 . Specific methods were shown in Additional file 1.

All data were subjected to normality tests. According to whether they complied with the normal distribution, the data underwent parametric or non-parametric tests. Since the data between groups were not paired and the standard deviations (SD) were not equal, unpaired t-tests with Welch correction were performed on all data. P < 0.05 was considered to indicate a significant difference between the two groups. GraphPad Prism 9.5.0 ( http://www.graphpad.com ) was used to analyze the data and draw bar charts and heat maps, and Origin 2021 ( https://www.originlab.com/MyOrigin2021Download ) was used to draw Sankey diagrams.

sections.discussion:
ETEC infection causes diarrhea in young animals, which is a matter of public health concern 3 , 4 . Our previous research findings indicated that ETEC infection damages the small intestinal barrier and triggers inflammatory stress and oxidative damage in the small intestines of weaned piglets, and that dietary berberine improves the homeostasis of gut microbiota, thereby alleviating the damages caused by the infection 12 , 23 . Microbes in the colon produce metabolites such as vitamins and short-chain fatty acids through a series of metabolic pathways 24 , 25 , these metabolites are absorbed and utilized by the colon, thereby affecting colonic reabsorption and subsequently influencing the animal body 26 , 27 . The microbial composition of the colon and small intestine differs, and the effects of berberine on the colon may vary from those on the small intestine. Thus, this study explored its impact on weaned piglet model infected with ETEC using colon metabolomics.

Hepatic function can be evaluated through traditional serum biomarkers, including AST, ALT, AST/ALT, and ALP. An elevated AST/ALT indicates hepatocyte necrosis 28 , and an increase in AST contents can more reliably reflect hepatic damage 29 . Reports have indicated that piglets infected with ETEC exhibit a significant increase in the CFU count of Escherichia coli in the liver, which is associated with liver damage 30 , 31 . In our study, ETEC infection significantly increases the contents of AST and AST/ALT in serum. This suggests the hepatic function was damaged in the piglets. Studies have found that berberine may affect the hepatic and intestines of weaned piglets infected with ETEC through mechanisms such as bile acid metabolism in the enterohepatic axis 11 , 32 . In our results, dietary berberine significantly decreased the contents of AST and AST/ALT in serum, suggesting that berberine relieved the hepatic injury in the piglets infected with ETEC.

The total protein content is an indicator of the animals’ immune status and protein metabolic capacity 33 – 35 . Serum total protein is mainly composed of albumin and globulin. Globin was divided into multiple types through different functions, and immunoglobulin is important in defense against bacterial infection 36 , 37 . Studies have shown that ETEC infection reduces the total protein and immunoglobulin content in the serum of weaned piglets, and the corresponding additives can alleviate this condition 38 , 39 . Conversely, our results show that ETEC infection increased the total protein and globulin contents in the serum of piglets and dietary berberine decreased these in the infected piglets. According to previous research, during ETEC infection, the contents of IgG and IgA were higher in the serum of piglets that ingested the colostrum of sows vaccinated with F4 fimbria vaccine 40 . In our experiment, two factors caused the increase in the total protein concentration in serum: first, piglets may produce more antibodies during ETEC attack; and second, the reabsorption of water was decreased in the large intestine. On the contrary, after berberine exerts its inhibitory effect on ETEC, the antibody content decreases to the normal level. In general, the hepatic function manages the synthesis of almost all plasma proteins in the body; however, changes in the protein content in serum suggest changes in the protein synthesis ability of the hepatic function 41 . ETEC infection affected the hepatic protein synthesis function of weaned piglets, and berberine relieved the change in hepatic protein synthesis function.

Lipids, including cholesterol and triglycerides, are absorbed in the intestines and transported throughout the body via lipoproteins for energy production, steroid synthesis, or bile acid formation 42 . Research shows that ETEC infection significantly reduces HDL in the serum of weaned piglets, while adding Lactobacillus plantarum can regulate pathways related to hepatic diseases 31 . Further research has found that the bile acid metabolism and hepatic function of weaned piglets infected with ETEC were damaged, increasing the triglyceride content in serum 43 , and berberine could alleviate the damage caused by ETEC 32 . Our results are consistent with those of these studies: In the serum of piglets, ETEC infection decreased the contents of total cholesterol, HDL, and LDL and increased the content of triglyceride, while dietary berberine increased the former and significantly decreased the latter. This suggests that berberine can relieve lipid metabolism disorders caused by ETEC infection.

Cytokines mediate signaling between cells based on their roles in inflammation. TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, IL-12, and IFN-γ were categorized as pro-inflammatory cytokines, which induce acute-phase responses and transmit inflammatory responses 44 . IL-4, IL-10, and TGF-β were categorized as anti-inflammatory cytokines that inhibit excessive inflammatory responses induced by pro-inflammatory cytokines 45 – 47 . Recent studies have shown that the levels of serum IL-6, IL-8, and TNF-α in the ETEC group were significantly increased 30 . ETEC infection increased the concentrations of TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6 and decreased the concentration of IL-10 in plasma 48 . In our results, ETEC infection increased the contents of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, IL-12, and IFN-γ) and anti-inflammatory cytokines (IL-4, IL-10, and TGF-β) in the serum of weaned piglets. The changes in pro-inflammatory cytokines are consistent with previous studies, while the change in IL-10 in anti-inflammatory cytokines is contrary to that by Wang 48 . In intestinal tissues, increases in the contents of TGF-β and IL-10 can protect piglets from severe infection and therefore inflammatory responses, which we have demonstrated in our previous studies 12 , 47 . It is reported that berberine can significantly inhibit the increase in pro-inflammatory cytokines in intestinal tissues 10 , 12 . In our results, dietary berberine decreased the contents of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, IL-12, and IFN-γ) in the serum of weaned piglets, suggesting that it alleviated the inflammatory response caused by ETEC infection.

Metabolomics holds vast potential for probing the functions within complex systems and broadening our understanding of gut microbial metabolism 14 . The complex metabolism in the colon produces a variety of metabolites that act on the animal itself, which can explain the changes in serum biochemical indicators 25 – 27 . Metabolomics provides a new approach to research on berberine. Compared with the BD + Saline group, the saccharin in the colon metabolism of weaned piglets infected with ETEC was downregulated. Sweeteners, such as saccharin, can inhibit the pathogen’s growth 49 . Experiments using guinea pigs as a model have shown that saccharin promotes physical development and intestinal health by modulating gut microbiota 50 . In addition, it can reduce the count of intestinal pathogens and reduce the colitis activity of mice 51 . The downregulation of saccharin suggests the growth and proliferation of pathogens in the intestines, and the impairment of intestinal health. Our results are consistent with previous studies in that hepatic function (total protein) and inflammation response (IFN-γ) were significantly correlated with saccharin, where the downregulation of saccharin after ETEC infection suggests inflammation in the piglet colon, compromised gut health, and poorer protein absorption and utilization. Current research on taste receptors suggests that sweet substances can bind to sweet receptors, thereby influencing the piglet’s nutritional sensing, monitoring energy storage changes, and triggering metabolic and behavioral responses 52 , 53 . In our study, ETEC infection may have impacted hepatic function and inflammatory response through taste transduction.

D-mannitol in the colon metabolism of weaned piglets infected with ETEC was downregulated. D-mannitol is another form of mannitol, which has certain immune regulatory functions 54 . While mannitol is often used to reduce intracranial and intraocular pressure, its absorption by the intestine is poor, and it is usually excreted with feces 55 . In our results, lipid metabolism (total cholesterol and LDL) and inflammation response (IL-1β, IL-8, and TGF-β) were significantly correlated with D-mannitol, whose downregulation in the colon may suggest that ETEC infection induces inflammatory changes and increases permeability in the colon. This intestinal inflammation can impair intestinal absorption capacity, thereby weakening the absorption of lipids. Mannitol, sorbitol, and mannose are metabolites derived from the metabolism of fructose, mannose, and galactose; fructose and mannose metabolism play important roles in regulating carbohydrate metabolism 56 . Due to the lack of complex metabolic enzymes in fructose metabolism, it is rapidly phosphorylated by ketohexokinase. Uncontrolled fructose catabolism can activate cellular signaling cascades and stimulate the excessive production of acetyl-CoA, which is converted to fatty acids. Moreover, when rapid ATP consumption, mediated by ketohexokinase, overwhelms ATP regeneration, AMP accumulates and initiates its catabolic pathway, leading to increased uric acid production 57 , 58 . High circulating uric acid contents were associated with oxidative damage, inflammation, and a variety of metabolic disorders 59 . Mannose metabolism is closely connected to glucose and fructose metabolism through isomerization reactions 57 , and studies have shown that increased mannose metabolism can alleviate metabolic disorder-associated steatohepatitis 60 . In our study, ETEC infection may have impacted lipid metabolism and inflammatory response through fructose and mannose metabolism.

Compared with the BD + ETEC group, the dihydroberberine in the colon metabolism of weaned piglets with dietary berberine was upregulated. Studies have shown that the gut microbiota can convert berberine into dihydroberberine via bacterial nitroreductase. This conversion promotes the intestinal absorption of berberine 61 , 62 . The structural analogs of berberine, such as dihydroberberine, may possess similar or even enhanced functions 63 . For instance, in mouse models of dextran sulfate sodium-induced ulcerative colitis, dihydroberberine has been demonstrated to exert protective effects by inhibiting immune-inflammatory responses and maintaining gut function 64 , which includes the digestion and absorption of proteins. Our results are consistent with these reports, hepatic function (total protein) and inflammatory responses (IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8 and IL-12) were significantly correlated with dihydroberberine, which may have improved the inflammatory response in weaned piglets infected with ETEC. The upregulation of dihydroberberine in the colonic metabolism of weaned piglets with dietary berberine confirms that berberine effectively transformed into an absorbable form in the intestines, thereby exerting its pharmacological effects. Therefore, in weaned piglets infected with ETEC, berberine enhanced intestinal protein absorption capacity and alleviated the inflammatory response in these piglets.

However, dihydroberberine was not correlated with metabolic pathways directly. In the correlation results with serum biochemical indicators, dihydroberberine shows the same performance as acetylcholine. Studies have shown that berberine has the potential to inhibit acetylcholinesterase and can decrease the hydrolysis of acetylcholine, so dihydroberberine may play a role in the metabolic pathways by decreasing the hydrolysis of acetylcholine 65 , 66 .

The acetylcholine in the colon metabolism of weaned piglets with dietary berberine was upregulated. Acetylcholine conveys cholinergic signals in regulating inflammatory and immune responses and has important functions as a vital cholinergic neurotransmitter 67 , 68 . For instance, previous research demonstrated that intracolonic administration of acetylcholine significantly improved colitis by promoting IL-10 secretion from monocytic myeloid-derived suppressor cells (M-MDSCs) and inhibiting inflammation via the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor/extracellular signal-regulated kinase (nAChR/ERK) pathway, and acetylcholine significantly decreased the mRNA expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines in the intestines of mice, including TNF-α, IFN-γ, IL-17 A, IL-1β, and IL-6 69 . Similarly, in our results, hepatic function (total protein) and inflammatory responses (IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, and IL-12) were significantly correlated with acetylcholine. The upregulation of acetylcholine in the colon may suggest that berberine alleviated the colonic inflammatory response.

Cholinergic receptors can be activated by acetylcholine, and cholinergic signaling has been shown to play a role in the physiological functions and the pancreas 70 , 71 . Pancreatic secretion and insulin secretion represent the exocrine and endocrine functions of the pancreas 72 , in which cytokines can modulate communication between different types of cells and changes in the immune microenvironment can impact diseases related to the pancreas, including pancreatic cancer, pancreatitis, and diabetes 73 . In our study, berberine may have alleviated inflammatory responses through pancreatic secretion and insulin secretion.

Acetylcholine released by the vagus nerve can lead to the secretion of gastric acid. The stomach’s acidic environment serves a dual purpose: it not only denatures proteins but also protects against potential pathogens 74 , 75 . The interaction between digestion-related cholinergic pathways and taste signaling pathways in parietal cells results in elevated cytosolic cAMP concentrations 76 . A substantial body of research has revealed that cAMP is involved in a wide variety of cellular functions to alleviate inflammation and prevent damage to the mucosal barrier 77 . In our study, berberine may have alleviated inflammatory responses through cholinergic synapses, taste transduction, and cAMP signaling pathway.

The anatomy and physiology of pig models are similar to those of the human intestine, and the study of weaned piglet models infected with ETEC has potential significance for clinical research on pediatric diarrheal diseases. Our findings suggest that berberine may alleviate the damage caused by ETEC infection through some common mechanisms, and these discoveries could provide support for research on the clinical application of berberine in childhood diarrheal diseases. However, the correlation between metabolite changes and physiological changes in the piglet model has not yet been experimentally validated, and further mechanistic studies are needed to elucidate whether these metabolic changes are causal drivers of the observed physiological responses or merely secondary associations.
sections.conclusion: ETEC infection and dietary berberine can induce changes in the colonic metabolites. ETEC infection causes lipid metabolism disorders and exacerbates the overall inflammatory response through fructose and mannitol metabolism pathways. Berberine alleviates the overall inflammatory response through various metabolic pathways mediated by cholinergic signals. It is worth noting that both induce changes in the taste transduction pathway. This may clarify the functions of berberine to promote its application in humans and provide a new approach to studying traditional Chinese herbal extracts.
